name: Yongning Na
catalog_citation: Michaud, Alexis. 2017. Tone in Yongning Na: Lexical tones and morphotonology (Studies in Diversity Linguistics 13). Berlin: Language Science Press. Open-access PDF, langsci-press.org/catalog/book/109.
catalog_quote: Prosody as defined here consists of (i) lexically distinctive properties: stress, as in English; tone, as in Mandarin, Yorùbá or Na; tonal accent, as in Japanese and Swedish; phonation-type register, as in Mon (Mon-Khmer family); (ii) intonation; and (iii) performance factors, including rhythm. ... To me, it is clear that Yongning Na is to be described as having a level-tone system ... A few general observations about information structure in Yongning Na will be followed by a discussion of three phenomena that belong to pragmatic intonation: (i) emphatic stress (§8.3.1), (ii) focalization through local intonational modification of tone (§8.3.2), and (iii) intonational backgrounding of function words (§8.5.1). ... the levelling rules of Yongning Na (Rules 4 and 5), whereby all tones following a H tone, or a M.L sequence, are lowered to L, have far-reaching consequences for surface phonol…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim in the Michaud 2017 text we hold at the stated printed/PDF pages (one footnote digit elided; one PDF-page slip 408->407 already logged by the second reader). (2) The classification 'tonal' (qv tonal-OR-pitch accent, domain phrase for the only 'stress' = emphatic/focus prosody) rests on a 2017 open-access 613-page tone monograph by the language's principal phonetician, cross-checked against the 922-page reference grammar (Lidz 2010), both. this is the best available description. (3) Four open HAL papers downloaded now (Michaud 2008 CLAO, Michaud 2015 BCL, Michaud & Brunelle 2016, Dobbs & La 2016 LTBA) all describe a level-tone system with lexical-item tone categories, tone-group domain, and prominence only as information-structure phrasing/emphatic stress - all confirm; Dobbs & La add that the Lataddi variety has two rather than three levels, which does not touch the s

sources.citation: Dobbs, Roselle & La Mingqing. 2016. The two-level tonal system of Lataddi Narua. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 39(1): 67-104 (HAL preprint halshs-02945164).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Lataddi variety of Narua (same glottocode) has 'only two tonal levels; all other Naish languages described to date have three. The language uses a system in which level tones are primary, and tones are associated to lexical items rather than to individual syllables'; prominence mentioned only as information-structure phrasing (citing Michaud 2015). Refines: dialectal variation in number of levels (2 vs 3), still tonal.

sources.citation: Michaud, Alexis & Marc Brunelle. 2016. Information Structure in Asia: Yongning Na (Sino-Tibetan) and Vietnamese (Austroasiatic). In Fery & Ishihara (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of Information Structure, ch. 40. OUP (HAL halshs-00945897).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Emphatic stress is found in Yongning Na... [it] can be considered an extreme form of focus prosody'; treated as intonational emphasis for information structure, not lexical/word stress.

sources.citation: Michaud, Alexis. 2015. Phrasing, prominence, and morphotonology: How utterances are divided into tone groups in Yongning Na. Bulletin of Chinese Linguistics 8: 112-152 (HAL halshs-01162331).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Three tonal levels (H, M, L); the tone group is 'the largest domain within which tonal computation takes place'; 'Prominence (conveying information structure) and phrasing (reflecting syntactic structure) interact in the division of an utterance into tone groups' - prominence is phrasal/informational, no word stress.
sources.locator: sec. 3 intro (HAL p.12 of 29) and sec. 3.5 (p.17)

sources.citation: Michaud, Alexis. 2008. Phonemic and tonal analysis of Yongning Na. Cahiers de Linguistique Asie Orientale 37(2): 159-196. doi:10.1163/1960602808x00064 (HAL halshs-00358610).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Yongning Na makes use of three tonal levels: H(igh), M(id) and L(ow)... tones in Na are not lexically associated with individual syllables. Each lexical item has a tonal pattern'; no mention of stress or accent anywhere in the article.
sources.locator: sec. 4 'An analysis of the tone system' (HAL txt l.860ff)
